rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all eight compounds and locate the elution window without risking a low-organic hold. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in both directions.

Double the gradient duration with all other settings fixed to identify which close pairs respond to slope. The first run's early final peak suggests this diagnostic run should remain near the ten-minute scoring threshold.

The shallower gradient resolves all but one pair; now change only temperature to test selectivity for that remaining overlap. Higher temperature should also create more room below the ten-minute time threshold.

Back off temperature by one step to separate the late-middle pair that approaches co-elution at 60 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged should preserve the other separations and keep the final peak below ten minutes.
Slightly flatten the gradient at the best-performing temperature to improve the remaining R = 1.10 pair. The current last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room for this adjustment without a time penalty.

The remaining overlap worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. This should improve that pair and shorten the run while testing whether the early-middle separations retain sufficient resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 6's gradient slope to adjust selectivity around the marginal R = 1.46 pair. This also removes some low-organic time while retaining substantial separation from the dead time for the first peak.

Slightly flatten injection 7's gradient to strengthen its two early-middle separations while using the remaining resolution margin in the later pairs. The lower endpoint remains above the observed elution window and provides finer slope adjustment on the instrument grid.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the R = 1.49 pair above threshold while preserving the later pair's margin. The endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak's estimated elution composition.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a slightly shallower slope to seek a shorter fully resolved run while compensating for compression of the early-middle peaks.

Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark and explore a lower-temperature selectivity regime for a potentially faster fully resolved method. The steeper gradient should offset some of the increased retention at 25 C.

Trim the low-temperature gradient's unused initial region to shorten retention and test whether the starting composition separates its remaining close pair. The endpoint stays well above the observed elution window, and injection 9 remains the fully resolved benchmark.

Shorten injection 12's gradient to test slope-driven separation of its only unresolved pair. This also tests a faster alternative to the maximum-score benchmark while checking the late pair's limited resolution margin.

Test temperature-driven selectivity at the faster gradient, since slope changes alone leave two pairs unresolved. Raising temperature should shorten retention further and may separate those pairs; injection 9 remains the maximum-score fallback.

At 25 C, raising the starting organic fraction shifted the central overlap toward separation; extend that adjustment while restoring a shallower slope to protect the late pair. This tests a shorter alternative while retaining injection 9 as the proven maximum-score method.

Slightly steepen injection 15's gradient to improve the R = 1.46 central pair while testing whether the late pair retains its small resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the last peak's estimated elution composition, and the run should shorten further.

Injection 16 achieves maximum CRF with the last peak at 4.63 minutes. Raise the starting organic fraction to seek a shorter separation, while slightly flattening the gradient to protect the late pair's narrow resolution margin.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing the R = 1.61 critical separation. Keep injection 17 as the benchmark if temperature compresses that pair below threshold.

Return to 25 C and test a narrower, higher-organic window to shorten the fastest fully resolved method. The shallower slope is intended to compensate for compression of the critical middle pair as the starting organic fraction rises.

Test a modest slope increase from 0.050 to 0.055 organic fraction per minute to find the speed limit near injection 17. Its critical R = 1.61 pair will determine whether this faster separation remains fully resolved.

The local slope increase lost full resolution, so retain injection 17 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark. Test a larger temperature shift to see whether the overlapping middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal, potentially enabling a substantially faster method.

Combine a lower starting organic fraction and shallower slope to restore the middle-pair separation lost at 30 C. This tests whether moderate heating can yield another fully resolved fast method; injection 17 remains the fastest proven benchmark.

Flatten the gradient at 30 C to recover the middle-pair separation while retaining the improved late-pair selectivity. This seeks a fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin; injection 17 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Increase the slope moderately from injection 23 to trade some of its resolution margin for a shorter separation. This intermediate slope should approach the R = 1.5 boundary without the severe overlap seen at the steeper 30 C gradient.
